The landscape of technology and science shifted significantly this week. Here are the developments you should know.

In the consumer tech space, Apple has made its biggest design change since 2007. The company unveiled the iPhone Duo, a folding, passport-sized device priced near $2,000. It marks the first major product test for new CEO John Ternus. Meanwhile, if you are planning to test out new software, remember that installing an iOS public beta requires a full data backup first to ensure your information remains secure.

Hardware constraints are impacting medical innovation. The head of chip designer Arm noted that a shortage of chips is currently slowing down AI research aimed at cancer treatment. While computers are expected to eventually solve complex DNA modelling, current capacity is limiting progress.

In the aerospace sector, a German startup called Isar Aerospace successfully launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe. This is a critical step for Europe as it tries to build independent access to space. On a larger scale, astronomers just released the most detailed map of the universe ever made. It covers 75 percent of the sky and features 4 billion celestial objects. Not to be outdone by Earth, Saturn has also revealed another mysterious, perfect geometric shape in its atmosphere, adding to the list of phenomena scientists are still working to understand.

Finally, in sustainability and automotive news, a new study offers good news for electric vehicle owners. Data suggests that EV batteries retain about 90 percent of their original capacity even after 150,000 km of driving. In the UK, a unique restoration project at Emblehope Moor is testing a new model for land acquisition. The plan aims to provide financial returns to investors before transferring ownership to community or charitable groups.

The James Webb Space Telescope is changing how we view the solar system.

By observing Chariklo, a small object tucked between Saturn and Uranus, researchers spotted something unexpected.

Over the course of just a few years, the rings surrounding this object have shifted in opacity. The inner ring has become more opaque, while the outer one has grown less so.

This suggests that the rings on smaller celestial bodies are far more dynamic than we previously assumed. It challenges the idea that these systems are stagnant or slow to change.
